{{< include _compose-kit.qmd >}}

A song is words and music working together. You can start from either one. Some writers start with a line of lyrics they like and find
the melody hidden in how it is spoken. Others start with a chord loop or a riff and sing nonsense syllables over it until words arrive.
Whichever comes first, the two have to fit, and this lesson is mostly about **how they fit**.

**How to use the page.** Press ▶ under a staff to hear the melody. The chorus example also has chords, so the band plays them with it, and
**▶ Chords** plays the chords alone.

## 1. Stress: the words already have a rhythm

Say this line out loud: *I can't stop thinking about you.* Some syllables are louder and longer than others:
*i CAN'T STOP THINK-ing a-BOUT you*. Those are the **stressed** syllables. Matching the words to the music is called **prosody**.
Good prosody puts the stressed syllables on strong beats or on notes that stand out (higher, longer). Then the line is sung the way it is spoken,
and it is easy to understand.

::: {.ax-pair}
<div class="abc-ex" data-bpm="92"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
T:Stresses on strong beats
M:4/4
L:1/8
K:C
z7 C | E2 E2 G2 F E | D2 C6 |]
w: I can't stop think-ing a-bout you
</script></div>

<div class="abc-ex" data-bpm="92"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
T:Stresses in the wrong places
M:4/4
L:1/8
K:C
z4 C E G A | c4 A2 G2 | E8 |]
w: I can't stop think-ing a-bout you
</script></div>
:::

In the second one, the long high note is on *-ing*, and *-bout* is squeezed onto a weak beat. It sounds like *thinkING aBOUT*. Singers can
force it, but listeners have to work to hear the words.

<div class="cp-tip">
<strong>Test it.</strong> Speak your line in time to a beat, clapping on the strong beats. The syllables you clap on are the ones that
should land on beats 1 and 3 (in 4/4). If you have to bend the word to make it fit, change the rhythm or change the word.
</div>

Prosody is wider than stress. The songwriter Pat Pattison describes it as the music supporting what the words say. A line about
falling can fall; a line about being stuck can stay on one note; a question can end up in the air, on a note that is not the tonic.

## 2. Lines and rhyme

Lyrics usually come in groups of lines (a verse, a chorus). How the lines rhyme gives the section its shape. Label each line's last sound with
a letter:

| Scheme | What happens | How it feels |
|---|---|---|
| **AABB** | lines 1 and 2 rhyme, then 3 and 4 | simple, settled, a bit nursery-rhyme |
| **ABAB** | lines 1 and 3, then 2 and 4 | flowing, the rhyme always pulls you on to the next line |
| **XAXA** | only lines 2 and 4 rhyme | the most common in songs: room to say what you mean in lines 1 and 3 |
| **AAAX** | three rhymes, then a line that doesn't | the odd line stands out: put the title or the twist there |

A **perfect rhyme** has the same vowel and the same ending (*go / slow*). A **near rhyme** shares only the vowel or only the ending
(*go / home*, *time / mine*). Most songwriters use both. A near rhyme often sounds less forced than a perfect one.

**Line length matters too.** Lines with the same number of stressed syllables can be sung to the same melody. If line 3 is much longer, the melody
has to change there, which can be good (contrast) or awkward (crowding).

## 3. Song form

Most popular songs are built from a few kinds of section:

- **Verse:** tells the story. The music is usually the same each time; the words change.
- **Pre-chorus** (optional): a short section that builds from the verse into the chorus.
- **Chorus:** the main message, with the **same words and music every time**. Usually the title is here.
- **Bridge:** a contrasting section, once, usually after the second chorus: new chords, new melody, a new angle on the lyric.

A common plan is *verse, chorus, verse, chorus, bridge, chorus*. An older one, the **AABA** or 32-bar form of many jazz standards and
show tunes, has four eight-bar sections: a melody (A), the same again (A), a contrasting **middle eight** (B), and the melody once more (A).
Practise naming the sections of songs you know with [Section Labels](section-labels.qmd).

## 4. The hook, and making the chorus different

A **hook** is the short idea a listener remembers: often the title, sung on a motif that repeats (see [Composing 2](compose-motif.qmd)).
Here is a four-bar chorus over the loop C, G, Am, F. Its two lines use the same rhythm, and the hook *hold on, hold on* opens both:

<div class="abc-ex" data-bpm="100" data-style="pop"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
T:A chorus hook: same rhythm, two lines
M:4/4
L:1/8
K:C
"C"G3 E G3 E | "G"d2 B2 G4 | "Am"A3 E A3 E | "F"A2 G2 F4 |]
w: Hold on, hold on, don't let go, Hold on, hold on, sing it slow.
</script></div>

The chorus has to sound like **arrival**. If the verse and chorus sound alike, the listener can't tell where the chorus starts. Change
something, or several things:

| | Verse | Chorus |
|---|---|---|
| **Register** | lower, closer to speech | higher: the melody's high point is usually here |
| **Rhythm** | more words, shorter notes | fewer words, longer notes |
| **Harmony** | can avoid the tonic, or start somewhere else | lands on the tonic, often on its first chord |
| **Arrangement** | thinner (see [Arranging 1](arrange-band.qmd)) | fuller: more instruments, drums open up |
| **Lyric** | details, story | the main idea, said simply |

## 5. Write a verse and a chorus

1. Write the chorus lyric first: two or four lines with the title in them. Speak it in time and mark the stresses.
2. Find a chord loop (see [Four-Chord Loops](four-chord-loops.qmd)), or use the one above.
3. Sing the chorus lyric over the loop several times, a different way each time. **Record each take on your phone.** Pick the best one and
   write down why it was the best.
4. Write the verse: lower, more words, and an ending that leads into the chorus.
5. Put it in the [Notation page](/tools/notation.qmd) with its words and chords (it reads ChordPro too), and hear it with the band.

Those recordings are evidence of your process. Keep them, give each a name and a date, and note which one you chose: see
[Process 1: Keeping a Process Journal](process-journal.qmd).

Next: [Composing 4: Instruments, Ranges and Transposing](compose-instruments.qmd).
